subject: 회의주의를 어떻게 다룰 것인가
title: Answering the doubt that swallows everything
content: A sceptical argument can be constructed against almost any body of belief. Perhaps your senses deceive you, perhaps your memory was created a moment ago, perhaps the world beyond your experience does not exist. Such arguments are not easily refuted, and yet nobody actually believes their conclusions, which makes them a peculiar kind of philosophical problem. The structure is always the same. A possibility is described in which everything seems exactly as it does now while your belief is false. Since you cannot rule that possibility out from where you stand, the argument concludes that you do not know what you took yourself to know. Each step looks acceptable and the conclusion is intolerable. One response attacks the demand. Knowledge, on this view, does not require eliminating every conceivable alternative but only the relevant ones, and a possibility nobody has reason to take seriously is not relevant. Critics reply that the sceptic has just given a reason, so the move looks like refusing to play. A second response reverses the argument. I know that I have hands; if I were being deceived I would not know that; therefore I am not being deceived. The premises are at least as plausible as the sceptic's, so the argument can be run in either direction, and which end one starts from is not itself settled by argument. A third response treats the doubt as idle. Beliefs are revised in response to evidence, and a hypothesis that predicts nothing and forbids nothing cannot be evidence against anything. What all these share is a refusal to accept that the burden lies entirely on the believer. The sceptic assumes that belief must be earned against every possibility, and that assumption, rather than any particular step, is where the real disagreement lies.

subject: 믿음은 의지로 정할 수 있는가
title: Whether you can decide what to believe
content: You can decide to raise your arm and then raise it. Try to decide to believe that it is raining when you can see that it is not, and nothing happens. Belief appears to be outside direct control in a way that action is not, and working out why has consequences for what we may demand of one another. The obvious explanation is that belief aims at truth. To believe something is to take it to be so, and one cannot take something to be so merely because it would be convenient, since the wanting has no bearing on the evidence. Anybody who could believe at will would find their beliefs disconnected from how things are, which would defeat the point of having them. If this is right, then a great deal of moral vocabulary applied to belief is misplaced. We criticise people for believing things, we call beliefs irresponsible, and we hold that somebody ought to have believed otherwise. Yet ought implies can, and if belief cannot be chosen, none of this can be literally correct. The usual repair locates the obligation elsewhere. What a person controls is inquiry: whether they look, how carefully, whom they consult, and whether they expose themselves to disagreement. Belief follows from that work, so the duty attaches to the process rather than to its result. On this reading somebody who believes badly is blamed for how they got there. Indirect control operates over longer periods. Choosing what to read, whom to spend time among, and which habits of attention to cultivate all shape what a person will find believable years later, and those are choices. The moral responsibility for belief is therefore real, delayed, and distributed across a life rather than exercised in any moment.

subject: 은유는 무엇을 하는가
title: How a comparison changes what you can think
content: Calling an argument an attack, or time a resource, or a theory a building, is so ordinary that it passes unnoticed. Philosophers once treated such expressions as decoration that could be replaced by literal statement without loss. That view has largely collapsed, and what replaced it changes how we understand thought itself. The first difficulty for the older view is that many metaphors cannot be paraphrased. Asked what a particular comparison means literally, speakers produce approximations that leave something out, and different speakers produce different approximations. If the metaphor were merely a compressed literal claim, unpacking it would be routine. The second difficulty is that metaphors come in systems. If argument is a contest, then positions are defended, points are scored, and objections are attacks, and the whole vocabulary hangs together. This suggests that the comparison is doing structural work rather than ornamenting a claim, since it supplies a way of organising a subject that has no shape of its own. The consequences are practical. A dispute framed as a battle is conducted differently from one framed as a joint search, and neither framing is neutral, so choosing a metaphor is partly choosing a conclusion. Debates about policy are frequently won by whichever comparison becomes standard, and the winning image is rarely examined. What follows for moral argument is a demand for attention. When somebody describes a burden as a debt, or a person as a resource, they have made a substantive claim under cover of a figure of speech, and the claim is hard to contest because it was never asserted. Making the comparison explicit is the first move in disagreeing with it, and it is a move that participants in public argument make far too rarely.

subject: 이름은 무엇을 집는가
title: How a name reaches its bearer
content: A name picks out one thing rather than another, and explaining how it manages this has proved surprisingly hard. The question matters beyond linguistics, since a great deal of argument turns on whether two people using one word are talking about the same thing. One traditional account says that a name works through a description the speaker associates with it. To use a name is to mean whatever satisfies that description, and this explains how a name can be informative, since learning that two names pick out one thing tells you something you did not know. The account faces a decisive objection. Speakers frequently hold false beliefs about whoever they are naming, and yet they succeed in referring. Somebody who believes only one false thing about a historical figure is still talking about that figure rather than about nobody, which the description account cannot allow. Worse, if a description determined the reference, then whoever happened to satisfy it would be the bearer, even if the speaker had never heard of them. A second account locates the mechanism in a chain. A name is attached to something at some initial occasion, and it passes from speaker to speaker with each intending to use it as those before them did. A person can therefore refer to somebody they know almost nothing about, because their use inherits its target from a history they never witnessed. The account extends to kinds of stuff. A word for a substance picks out whatever shares the nature of the original samples, so speakers who could not tell that substance from a lookalike were nonetheless talking about it. This yields a striking conclusion: certain truths about what things are turn out to be necessary while being discoverable only by investigation.

subject: 대표한다는 것의 의미
title: What a representative is supposed to do
content: Somebody elected to act for others faces a question that the office itself does not answer. Should they do what those who chose them want, or what they judge best? Both answers have serious defenders, and although the dispute is old, it runs through every argument about how a democracy ought to work. The first position treats them as a delegate. Their power comes from those who sent them, and because they hold no separate mandate, putting their own view first defeats the point of the whole arrangement. On this reading a representative who votes against the clear preference of those they represent has taken something that was not theirs. The second position treats them as a trustee instead. They were chosen for their judgment, and since they hear argument that the public does not, somebody who merely counts opinions adds nothing that a survey could not supply. Its most famous statement holds that a representative owes constituents their industry and their judgment, and betrays them by sacrificing the second. Yet each position becomes uncomfortable in particular cases. The first view requires backing measures they believe harmful, and some of that harm falls on people who could not vote at all. The trustee view licenses ignoring a settled and informed public preference, which is difficult to distinguish from simply substituting one's own values. A further difficulty concerns whom they represent. Those who voted for them, everybody in the district, or the whole community affected are different constituencies with different claims, and the answer changes the analysis entirely. What this argument establishes is that being elected does not by itself settle the relation. A system must decide what it wants representatives to be, and most systems have never decided explicitly, which is why the same conduct is praised as principled and condemned as arrogant by people applying different unstated theories.

subject: 공유지는 어떻게 지켜지는가
title: When shared resources are not destroyed
content: A famous argument holds that resources held in common will be exhausted. Each user gains from taking more while the cost of depletion is shared, so everybody takes and the resource fails. The reasoning is clear, and the empirical record turns out to be considerably more interesting than the argument predicts. Field studies of fisheries, forests, irrigation systems, and pastures found many communities that had used a shared resource for centuries without exhausting it. These were not cases of central control or private division, which are the two remedies the argument recommends. They were cases where users had worked out their own rules and enforced them among themselves. The successful arrangements share recognisable features. The boundaries of the resource and of who may use it are clear. The rules match local conditions rather than being imposed uniformly. Those affected participate in making them. Monitoring is done by the users themselves or by people accountable to them, and penalties start small and increase with repetition rather than beginning at the maximum. Disputes have a cheap forum, and the right to organise is recognised by outside authorities. The failures are equally instructive. Arrangements collapse where outsiders can enter freely, where the state overrides local rules with its own, and where the resource is so large that monitoring is impossible. The original argument therefore describes a real case rather than a universal law, and the case it describes is unmanaged open access rather than common property. What follows for policy is that the two standard remedies are not the only options. Communities can and do govern shared resources, and institutions that assume they cannot frequently destroy arrangements that were working, which is a failure that the confident version of the argument helped to produce.

subject: 추첨으로 뽑는 대표
title: Choosing officials by drawing lots
content: Selecting people for public office by lot sounds absurd to modern ears, and it was the standard method in the democracy that gave us the word. Most positions in classical Athens were filled by drawing from those willing to serve, and election was reserved for a few roles where expertise was thought essential. Recovering the reasoning behind that arrangement is worthwhile. The argument was about equality. If every citizen is equally entitled to rule, then any method that systematically advantages some over others introduces an aristocracy. Election does exactly this, since it rewards wealth, reputation, connection, and the leisure to campaign, and the ancient writers who compared the two methods said so directly. Drawing lots is the only procedure that treats everybody identically. A second argument concerned corruption. Somebody who cannot know in advance who will hold an office cannot buy them, and somebody who serves briefly and returns to ordinary life has weaker reason to build a durable network of favours. Short terms combined with random selection made the accumulation of personal power considerably harder. The obvious objection is competence. A randomly chosen person may know nothing about the matter before them, and the ancient system answered this with training, with advisory bodies, and by reserving technical offices for election. Modern experiments have answered it differently, supplying selected panels with expert briefing and extended deliberation. Such panels have been used in several countries to consider constitutional questions that elected bodies could not resolve, and their reports have been notably less partisan than parliamentary debate. Whether the method could carry more weight than that remains genuinely open, although the reasoning behind it — that election is not the same thing as democracy — deserves more attention than it usually receives.

subject: 화성이 굳어 온 과정
title: How chords came to sound inevitable
content: A listener raised on European music hears some chord moves as closed and others as open. That sense of arrival feels like a fact about sound, and it is what is left of several centuries in which one way of stacking notes hardened into a system. The starting point was melodic rather than chordal. Early part music joined free lines, and the gaps that fell between them were ruled by which pairs were allowed at strong beats. Harmony in the modern sense — chords as units with jobs — was not the ruling idea, and describing that music in chord terms bends what its makers were doing. The shift happened gradually across the seventeenth century. A bass line with figures marking the harmony above it became normal, which meant players were now thinking in stacks, and writers began describing moves between chords rather than meetings between lines. Once that description existed, composers wrote to it. The system reached its tightest form in the eighteenth century, with each chord given a job in relation to a home note and a few moves treated as normal. Music teaching has passed that system on ever since, which is why students often take it to describe music at large rather than one tradition in one era. Its dissolution began almost as soon as it was complete. Composers of the nineteenth century stretched the relationships until the centre became ambiguous, and those of the twentieth abandoned the framework entirely or built alternatives. Yet the trained expectation persists, and popular music of the past century works almost entirely within it, which is why a progression written three hundred years ago still sounds like an arrival.

subject: 지휘자는 왜 생겼는가
title: The figure who plays nothing
content: An orchestra of the eighteenth century managed without anybody standing in front of it waving a stick. Its direction came from the keyboard player or the leading violin, who set the pace and cued entries while playing. The separate conductor is a nineteenth century arrival, and seeing why this role appeared explains much of what it actually does. Sheer size was the first cause of it. As these groups grew past what one player could hold together from inside, and as halls grew larger, players on opposite sides could no longer hear each other well enough to keep time. Somebody visible to everybody, doing nothing but indicating time, solved a problem that had not existed at smaller scale. Their music changed too. Scores began requiring frequent changes of tempo, sudden shifts of character, and precise balance among many parts, and these are decisions rather than mechanical tasks. A work with one steady pulse can run itself; one that pushes on, holds back, and shifts its weight needs a single judgment applied throughout, and that is why this role became a reading of the music rather than a mere service. Authority followed from that. Conductors acquired power over hiring, programming, and rehearsal, and the nineteenth century produced the figure of the maestro whose reading of a work was the point of attending. Recordings intensified this, since a listener chooses among versions identified by the conductor rather than by the orchestra. There has been a counter movement against this. Ensembles playing earlier repertoire frequently direct themselves from within, arguing that the music was written for that arrangement and sounds different when it is imposed from outside. Several modern groups perform without a conductor entirely, which requires far more rehearsal and produces an ensemble that listens differently, and audiences report hearing the difference.

subject: 라디오가 만든 청취 습관
title: When music arrived without being asked for
content: Before broadcasting, hearing music required going where it was performed or making it yourself. Radio changed the relation completely, delivering sound into a room where somebody was doing something else, and the habits that formed around that arrangement still govern how most people encounter music. Attention became optional. A concert demands that an audience sit still and listen; a broadcast plays while a listener cooks, works, or talks, so music became an accompaniment to other activity for the first time in its history. Composers and critics of the period argued about whether this was a democratisation or a degradation, and both descriptions were partly right. Repertoire narrowed and widened at once. Broadcasters reached audiences who had never heard an orchestra, and the same broadcasters, needing to hold those audiences, favoured works that were immediately attractive. Familiar pieces were repeated while difficult ones appeared rarely, so a canon formed that was shaped by what worked on air rather than by any critical judgment. The scheduling itself became a cultural force. Programmes at fixed hours gathered audiences who listened together without being together, and the shared experience of a national broadcast created a common repertoire across a whole country within a generation. Countries that established public broadcasters with an educational mandate produced measurably different musical cultures from those that left it to advertisers. What survives most strongly is the expectation of background sound. Shops, restaurants, and workplaces play music continuously, and the practice began with broadcasting rather than with any older tradition. Listening with full attention has become the exception rather than the norm, which reverses the situation of every previous century and changes what composers can assume about how their work will be heard.

subject: 자연법칙이란 무엇인가
title: What makes a regularity a law
content: Some patterns in the world are called laws and others are merely true. Every sphere of enriched uranium is smaller than a kilometre across, and so is every sphere of gold, and yet only the first seems to reflect something that had to be so. Explaining the difference is a central problem in the philosophy of science. One account holds that laws are simply the regularities appearing in the best systematisation of everything that happens. Among all the ways of summarising the world, one achieves the finest balance of simplicity and strength, and whatever appears as an axiom in that system counts as a law. This requires nothing mysterious, and it explains why accidental regularities are excluded, since they earn no place in an economical summary. Critics find it unsatisfying. On this account the laws depend on what happens to occur, and yet we take laws to govern what occurs rather than to be summarised by it. A universe with very few events would have laws that reflected its poverty, which seems to reverse the direction of dependence. A second account posits relations between properties themselves. If being one property necessitates being another, then the corresponding regularity holds because of that relation, and it would have held whatever particular events had occurred. This delivers the governing character we wanted at the cost of introducing entities nobody can observe, and explaining how such a relation produces a regularity has proved difficult. A third position denies that laws are fundamental at all, treating them as tools for prediction rather than descriptions of a hidden order. What the dispute reveals is that a notion working perfectly well inside the sciences becomes obscure the moment anybody asks what it means.

subject: 자장가의 보편성
title: The song every culture invented
content: Songs sung to infants appear in every culture that has been studied, and they resemble one another to a degree that almost no other musical form matches. The tempo is slow, the range is narrow, phrases repeat, and the contour tends to fall. Listeners can identify a lullaby from an unfamiliar tradition at rates far above chance, which is unusual for any kind of music. The convergence has an obvious explanation, and it is worth stating carefully. Such songs are addressed to a listener with no cultural training whatever, so they cannot rely on learned conventions and must work on whatever an infant responds to. Everything that varies across traditions is therefore stripped away, leaving features that operate before any tradition has been absorbed. The functional demands are narrow. The singer needs to hold attention gently rather than excite it, to be sustainable for a long period, and to be performable while doing something else, since a person singing to a child is usually also holding one. A slow repetitive song within a comfortable range meets all three, and a lively one meets none. Texts diverge completely where the music converges. Lullabies frequently carry material that has nothing to do with comfort — complaints about labour, grief, warnings, and in several traditions frank descriptions of hardship — because the singer is alone with somebody who cannot understand the words. Collectors have noted that these songs preserve testimony available nowhere else in a tradition. What the form demonstrates is a boundary between the universal and the cultural. The music is shaped by an audience that has learned nothing; the words are shaped by a singer who can say anything, and the two halves of the same song sit on opposite sides of that line.

subject: 악기 제작 장인의 세계
title: Making the instrument that somebody else will play
content: Instrument making is a craft with an unusual relation to its result. The maker never produces the sound; a player does, years later, and the maker may never hear it. Judging one's own work therefore requires imagining what somebody else will do with it, which is a form of skill that few other crafts demand. Material selection carries most of the outcome. Wood varies in density and stiffness within a single tree, and makers select and orient pieces by tapping, flexing, and looking at the grain, judgments that resist measurement and that experienced makers describe as reading rather than testing. Two instruments built to identical dimensions from different pieces of wood will not sound alike. The most celebrated instruments of the past have been examined exhaustively without settling why they are admired. Proposals have included the varnish, the density of the timber, chemical treatments, and the climate during the trees' growth, and controlled listening tests have repeatedly failed to distinguish them from good modern instruments when players and listeners cannot see what is being played. That result is disputed within the profession and it has not changed the market. Repair is the other half of the craft. Instruments in use for centuries have been altered repeatedly — necks reset, bass bars replaced, fingerboards lengthened — to meet changing demands for volume and range, so almost no old instrument is in its original condition. A restorer must decide what state to preserve, which is the same question that faces anybody conserving an object still in use. The training remains an apprenticeship. Schools exist, and the essential judgments are still transmitted by working beside somebody who has them, because nobody has found a way to write down what a piece of wood should feel like.

subject: 물감의 화학과 색의 역사
title: Why painters could not paint certain colours
content: The colours available to a painter have never been a matter of choice alone. Each pigment is a substance with a source, a price, and a set of behaviours, and the history of painting is partly a history of what could be obtained and what it did once applied. Ultramarine is the standard example. Made by grinding a stone quarried in one region of central Asia, it cost more than gold by weight in medieval Europe, and contracts specify how much a patron would supply and where it was to be used. Its reservation for the most important figure in a picture was an economic fact before it became a convention, and the convention outlived the cost when a synthetic version arrived in the nineteenth century. Other colours were unavailable rather than expensive. A stable bright yellow, a reliable green, and a purple that did not fade were genuine problems, and painters worked around them by glazing one transparent layer over another to produce hues that no single pigment could supply. Some of these combinations have since darkened or separated, so pictures now show relationships their makers never intended. Chemistry transformed the palette across the nineteenth century. New pigments appeared in quantity, sold ready mixed in tubes rather than ground in the studio, and painters could suddenly work outdoors with a full range of colour. The movements that followed are inseparable from that change, since painting a landscape on site in bright colour was not previously possible. Conservation now works backwards through this history. Identifying a pigment dates a picture, exposes later restoration, and occasionally exposes a forgery, since a colour that did not exist when a work was supposedly painted is difficult to explain away.

subject: 환원과 창발
title: Whether the whole is just its parts
content: A living cell is made of molecules and nothing else. Whether everything true of the cell can therefore be stated in terms of molecules is a different question, and the answer determines how the sciences relate to one another. Reduction is the claim that higher level facts hold in virtue of lower level ones and can in principle be explained by them. Its strongest support is that nothing extra seems to be present. Nobody has found a component of a living thing that is not chemical, and explanations of biological processes in chemical terms have succeeded repeatedly, which is a substantial record. Emergence is the claim that some properties belong to arrangements rather than to parts, and cannot be derived from the parts alone. A weak version says only that we cannot in practice do the derivation, which nobody disputes. A strong version says the derivation is impossible in principle, and defending that has proved hard, since it seems to require that something be present which the components do not supply. A middle position denies that the question has one answer. Explanation is relative to what somebody is trying to understand, and an account at the level of molecules may be perfectly correct while answering no question anybody asked. Why a population declined is answered by predation and food supply, and a molecular account of every organism involved would contain that answer without stating it. What this suggests is that the sciences are not arranged in a hierarchy waiting to be collapsed. Each level has its own regularities, and those regularities are real even if they depend on lower ones, which is why a chemist and an ecologist studying the same forest are not doing the same work at different resolutions.

subject: 프레스코가 강요하는 속도
title: Painting that must be finished before it dries
content: Fresco requires pigment to be applied to plaster while the plaster is still wet. As it cures, the colour is bound into the wall itself rather than sitting on top of it, which produces exceptional durability and imposes a schedule that no other painting technique demands. The plaster sets within a day. A painter therefore works on an area sized to what can be completed in that time, and the boundaries between one day's work and the next are visible in raking light on almost every surviving fresco. Scholars count these divisions to reconstruct how long a wall took and how the labour was organised, which makes the technique unusually informative about workshop practice. Correction is nearly impossible. Once the surface has set, altering it means cutting out the plaster and starting that section again, so the design must be resolved before work begins. Full size drawings were prepared and transferred to the wall by pricking the outlines and dusting powder through the holes, and surviving cartoons show how completely the composition was fixed in advance. Improvisation happened, and it happened at cost. The palette is constrained as well. Only pigments that survive contact with lime can be used, which excludes several important colours, so certain hues had to be added after the plaster dried using a different binder. Those additions are the first thing to be lost, which is why many frescoes now show gaps in precisely the areas that once carried the strongest colour. What the technique produces is a particular kind of surface. Colour sits within the wall rather than upon it, the light passes into the plaster before returning, and the resulting luminosity is not obtainable by any method that lays paint on top of a prepared ground.

subject: 미술 아카데미의 교육
title: How painters were taught for three centuries
content: From the sixteenth century onward, European painting was taught in schools with a set course of study. The academies established a sequence that remained essentially unchanged for three hundred years, and understanding it explains both the achievements of that tradition and the reaction that eventually destroyed it. Because a beginner cannot yet see accurately, this sequence began with copying. Students drew from prints and drawings by established masters, then from plaster casts of ancient sculpture, and only afterwards from a living model. Each stage lasted years, and although a gifted student might move faster, progression was controlled, so a decade could pass before they painted anything of their own. The reasoning was that a beginner cannot see accurately and must be trained by copying work in which the difficult judgments have already been made. Subject matter was ranked as well. Historical and religious compositions with multiple figures stood at the top, followed by portraiture, then everyday scenes, then landscape, with still life at the bottom, and the hierarchy determined prizes, commissions, and prices. A painter's standing depended on the category they worked in as much as on the quality of the work. Therefore the system produced formidable technical skill, although it also narrowed the sense of what painting was for. Its authority rested on controlling exhibition, because a jury decided what the public would see, and rejection could end a career. The revolts of the nineteenth century were directed at the jury as much as at the teaching. Yet what replaced it was not a different course of study but the absence of one. Modern art education abandoned the sequence, and the skills it produced became rare within a generation, which some regard as a loss and others as the price of removing a gatekeeper whose judgments had become predictable and provincial.

subject: 사고 실험은 무엇을 보여주는가
title: Reasoning from cases that never happened
content: Philosophy relies heavily on imagined scenarios. A runaway vehicle, a person in a windowless room, a machine supplying any experience: such cases are described, a judgment is elicited, and conclusions are drawn about what our concepts require. Whether anything can be learned this way is a fair question. The defence is that these are arguments rather than experiments. Nothing is being observed; a case is constructed so that one factor is isolated from everything that normally accompanies it, and the resulting judgment shows what that factor contributes. Ordinary situations bundle considerations together, and the artificiality is precisely what separates them. Physics uses frictionless planes for the same reason. The objections are serious. Cases described in a few sentences are radically underspecified, so readers fill in the details differently and then find that they disagree about the verdict when they are actually considering different situations. Judgments about scenarios far from ordinary experience may simply be unreliable, since the intuitions being consulted were formed under conditions the case has removed. And the described case may be impossible in ways the description conceals. A further worry concerns selection. A philosopher constructs the case that elicits the verdict they expect, and cases that would elicit the opposite are not constructed, so the method can confirm almost anything if the practitioner controls the examples. This is a real risk and it is answerable by inviting rivals to build their own cases. What emerges is a modest defence. Such cases test whether a stated principle delivers acceptable verdicts, which is genuine work, and they establish very little on their own. Treating one arresting scenario as settling a moral question mistakes a probe for a proof, and a great deal of confident argument has made exactly that mistake.

subject: 화상이 만든 미술 시장
title: The dealer who invented the modern artist
content: For most of European history a painter worked to commission. A patron specified the subject, the size, the materials, and frequently the schedule, and the contract survives for many major works. The arrangement in which an artist produces what they choose and a dealer finds a buyer afterwards is comparatively recent, and it changed what artists could make. Dealers appeared as an intermediate class in the seventeenth century and became central in the nineteenth. The decisive innovation was the exclusive contract, under which a dealer paid an artist regularly in exchange for their entire output. This freed the painter from finding buyers and gave the dealer an interest in raising prices over time, which meant promoting a reputation rather than selling individual pictures. Several movements now regarded as central to modern art were sustained by exactly this arrangement. Artists rejected by official exhibitions had no other route to an audience, and a dealer willing to show and defend unsold work for years made their careers possible. The commercial relation and the artistic independence arrived together, which complicates any account that treats the market as purely a constraint. The costs are equally clear. A dealer's judgment determines what reaches the public, prices respond to scarcity and reputation rather than to any quality of the work, and an artist whose output is contracted has a reason to keep producing what sells. Critics have argued since the nineteenth century that the system rewards a recognisable signature style over development. What the history shows is that the modern conception of the artist — working without commission, judged by a body of work rather than by individual objects, discovered rather than employed — is inseparable from a particular commercial arrangement that began as a way of managing risk.

subject: 추상으로 넘어가던 시기
title: When pictures stopped showing things
content: Painting that shows nothing appeared in Europe within a few years around 1910, in several countries and among artists with little contact. That they arrived at once suggests that conditions rather than single invention were decisive, and setting out those conditions explains a change that still puzzles many viewers. Photography had taken away a job. Painting no longer had to record how things look, and painters had spent fifty years trying what else it could do — the surface, the mark, the way colour is laid out — so the subject had already grown less central before it was dropped. The step from a barely readable subject to none at all was smaller than it now looks. Music gave them the model. Music without words shows nothing and still moves people, which the first such painters cited again and again as proof that an art can reach an audience without picturing a thing. Several used musical vocabulary in their titles, and one wrote extensively on correspondences between colour and sound. Ornament gave them another precedent, since pattern had never pictured anything, though its low standing made the comparison awkward for painters claiming a serious aim. Two directions opened almost at once. One went after geometry, cutting back to straight lines and primary colours in search of a shared visual order. The other pursued gesture, treating the mark as a direct record of the maker. Both continue. Audience resistance was and remains substantial, and it usually rests on a reasonable question: if a picture shows nothing, what distinguishes a good one from a bad one? The tradition's answer concerns relations among elements rather than fidelity to a subject, which is a standard that requires training to apply and cannot be verified by comparison with anything outside the work.

subject: 사진을 오려 붙이는 미술
title: Cutting photographs apart to make an argument
content: Photomontage assembles pieces of photographs into an image that was never photographed. The technique appeared shortly after the First World War and was used immediately for political attack, which is unusual among modern art forms and follows directly from what the material carries. A photograph brings its own authority. Viewers treat it as evidence in a way they do not treat a drawing, so combining photographic fragments produces something that looks like a record while asserting a relation that no camera observed. Placing a politician's head on another body, or a machine inside a domestic scene, makes a claim with the force of documentation, and that borrowed force is the technique's essential resource. The most celebrated practitioners worked as propagandists rather than as gallery artists. Their pieces appeared on magazine covers and posters, addressed current events, and were designed to be understood in seconds by people with no interest in art. Several were produced in exile and smuggled into the country they attacked, which indicates how seriously the work was taken by its targets. The method also served purposes that were not polemical. Artists used it to represent the experience of a modern city, where unrelated images arrive simultaneously from advertising, print, and the street, and the fractured surface was defended as more accurate to that experience than any unified picture could be. What has changed since is the ease. Assembling a convincing composite once required a darkroom and considerable skill, and now requires neither, so the technique has moved from the studio into ordinary circulation. The consequence is that the photographic authority the form exploited has been substantially eroded, and an art built on the credibility of the photograph now operates in a world where nobody quite believes one.

subject: 통계적 유의성의 오용
title: A threshold that was never meant to decide anything
content: A result is commonly reported as significant when a particular calculated quantity falls below a conventional threshold. Enormous consequences follow from that line — publication, funding, policy — and the reasoning behind it is far weaker than the practice suggests. The quantity answers a narrow question: how surprising the observed data would be if a specified hypothesis were true and everything about the study were as assumed. It does not give the probability that the hypothesis is false, nor that the effect is real, nor that it matters. These misreadings are so common that professional bodies have issued statements correcting them, with limited effect. The threshold itself was proposed as a convenience and explicitly described by its originator as a matter of judgment rather than a rule. Treating it as a boundary between discovery and nothing produces two errors at once. A result just inside is reported as established while one just outside is reported as absent, although the difference between them may itself be well within noise. Incentives make matters worse. Since results below the line are publishable and those above it are not, researchers face pressure to reach it, and the flexibility available in analysis is usually sufficient to get there. The published literature is therefore a filtered sample, and the filter selects for exactly the results most likely to be false. Replication failures across several fields have been traced to this mechanism. The proposed remedies are procedural rather than statistical: registering the analysis before collecting data, reporting the size of an effect with its uncertainty rather than a verdict, and publishing regardless of outcome. What none of them supplies is the thing the threshold appeared to offer, which was a way of deciding without judgment, and the appeal of that offer explains why the practice has survived decades of criticism.

subject: 퍼포먼스를 기록한다는 것
title: Documenting an art that exists only while it happens
content: Performance art is made in real time before an audience and then stops. Nothing remains except whatever was recorded, and the relation between the event and its documentation has been argued about since the form emerged, because the argument concerns what the work actually is. One position holds that the performance is the work and the documentation is a trace. Photographs and film misrepresent it, since they fix one angle and one moment from something that surrounded its audience and unfolded in duration. On this view anybody encountering only the record has not experienced the work, and the record's aesthetic qualities are beside the point. The opposing position notes that almost everybody encounters these works through documentation, that many were photographed with considerable care, and that in several cases the surviving image was composed deliberately for the camera with no audience present. If the photograph was planned as the outcome, then treating it as a mere trace misdescribes what the artist made. Both positions describe real cases, and practice varies. Some artists refuse recording entirely, some perform for an audience and permit documentation afterwards, and some construct events that exist principally as images. The question is therefore not general but specific to each work and each artist's stated intention. Institutions face the practical version. A museum acquiring such a work is buying instructions, materials, rights, or a video, and must decide what it now holds and how it may be shown. Several have commissioned re-performances by other people, which raises the further question of whether a work tied to one body can be performed by another. The answers vary by artist, and the disagreements among them are part of what the form has produced.

subject: 벽화 운동과 공공성
title: Painting on walls for people who never enter galleries
content: Mural movements have appeared again and again wherever artists decided that painting had become a private good. Their reasoning holds across very different settings: a picture on a wall is seen by everybody who passes, cannot be bought, and speaks to people who would never enter a gallery. The Mexican movement of the twentieth century is its fullest example. State orders covered public buildings with works telling the national story, and its artists argued openly that a canvas serves a collector while a wall serves a public. Their size, their plainness, and their subjects followed from that argument rather than from any taste in method. The approach spread from there. Government programmes in the United States during the same decades covered post offices and schools, community movements later covered walls in neighbourhoods that had commissioned nothing, and comparable movements appeared across several continents. In each case the work was made where people already were rather than where art was displayed. Their difficulties are equally consistent. A public work must be legible to a mixed audience, which limits what it can attempt, and murals commissioned by a state tend toward the version of history that state prefers. Community projects face a different problem, since the community rarely agrees about what should be shown, and the process of deciding frequently takes longer than the painting. Lasting is the last of these difficulties. Walls are demolished, painted over, and weathered, and murals are among the least durable painting despite being the most public. Several celebrated works have been lost to redevelopment, and conservation of an object that belongs to nobody in particular has no obvious funder, which is the ordinary cost of making art that escaped the market.
